notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to your Calf Muscle Strain Rehab Plan

This is a rehabilitation program for anyone who has suffered from a nerve-related calf muscle strain.

There is a big difference between a “calf muscle strain” and a “calf muscle tear” , so it is vital that you have the correct diagnosis before you start a rehab plan.

Make sure you read THIS ARTICLE on how to diagnose your calf muscle injury correctly before you start following this plan.

When is your calf muscle ready to start this plan?

You can begin this program as soon as you’re able to walk normally without pain—this is usually within 1–2 days after a minor calf strain. If you’re still limping after 3 or 4 days, it’s possible you’re dealing with a more serious calf tear. In that case, our Calf Muscle Tear Rehab Plan would be more appropriate for you.

There is no running during the first 10 days of this plan. Instead, you’ll focus on a series of stretches and gentle exercises designed to improve mobility and flexibility in your lower back, hips, calves, and sciatic nerve. This work is a crucial part of your recovery and will help get your body ready to return to running safely and confidently by Day 10.

NB: You need a massage ball for the stretching workout.

NB: If you have an un-diagnosed calf muscle injury which isn’t improving as quickly as you would expect, we highly recommend you seek advice from a registered medical professional.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
In Week 1, there will be no running, so we won’t yet be focusing on your running technique. Instead, we’ll concentrate on improving the mobility in your lower back, hips, ankles, and calf muscles, as well as enhancing the mobility of your sciatic nerve. This week is all about laying a solid foundation with a stretching routine that will help loosen up those key areas and start the recovery process. Take your time and make sure you’re performing the stretches properly. If you have enough time and feel comfortable, you can aim to complete the routine twice a day this week. Remember to start gently – the goal is to ease into it without stirring anything up.

Next week, we’ll also be introducing a strength and stability workout to support your body maintenance routine. Let’s get started!

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
The Role of Nutrition in Recovery

What you eat for the duration of this training plan can make a real difference to how quickly your calf muscle heals. A healthy, nutrient-rich diet helps to reduce inflammation in your body and supports the repair of damaged tissues. Focus on eating plenty of colourful vegetables, lean proteins, healthy fats (like those from nuts, seeds, and oily fish), and whole grains. These foods provide the vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants your body needs to recover efficiently. Drinking enough water is also essential to keep your muscles hydrated and your tissues supple. Think of your meals this week as fuel for healing—every good choice gives your body a better chance of bouncing back faster.

Read THIS ARTICLE which goes into more depth about how your diet can help to reduce inflammation

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week two of your Calf Muscle Strain Rehab Plan

This week we are going to continue with the same stretching and trigger point ball routine from week 1. We are also going to add some “core” exercises which will help to improve the strength and the stability of the muscles around your hips and pelvis. A stronger core will help to prevent a recurrence of the calf muscle strain.

Running

Return to Running Intervals – Starting on Day 10 (Wednesday)

We’ll ease back into running on Day 10 of your rehab, using interval-style sessions that include walking breaks. This isn’t just to take it easy—it’s a key strategy in preventing re-injury.

Calf strains usually worsen when tension builds up during continuous running. By inserting short walking breaks, we help reset that tension, giving your body a mini fresh start with each interval.

For example, many runners can comfortably complete 2 minutes running / 1 minute walking for 30–40 minutes total without issues. But if they run 15 minutes nonstop, the calf might flare up again. That’s why we take this gradual approach.

Yes, walking breaks can feel frustrating—but they actually allow you to maximise your running volume while still allowing you to recover faster. This controlled, step-by-step method is the safest and fastest way to return to full running fitness.

Each week, we’ll gently increase your total running time. Here’s how it works:

- Run 1 min / Walk 1 min x 5 reps means: run for 1 minute at a comfortable pace, walk for 1 minute, and repeat this cycle 5 times.

Run 1 min / Walk 1 min x 5 reps means: run for 1 minute at a comfortable pace, walk for 1 minute, and repeat this cycle 5 times.

- If your calf starts to feel tight during the session, stop immediately. Rest for that day, do the stretching routine and then try the same running session again the next day.

If your calf starts to feel tight during the session, stop immediately. Rest for that day, do the stretching routine and then try the same running session again the next day.

- You must complete each interval level twice without tightness or pain before progressing to the next level (e.g., from 5 reps to 7 reps).

You must complete each interval level twice without tightness or pain before progressing to the next level (e.g., from 5 reps to 7 reps).

- If tightness returns, repeat the previous level until you’re symptom-free.

If tightness returns, repeat the previous level until you’re symptom-free.

Everyone recovers at their own pace, so while this is a 10-week plan, your timeline may vary depending on how your calf responds. The key is to listen to your body and progress gradually.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Running Technique

A vital component in not re-straining your calf muscle is to ensure you are running with good technique. Poor running technique, over striding in particular, puts more stress on your glute muscles and creates more load/compression on the sciatic nerve.

This week we are going to focus on improving your running technique. Watch the video below to learn more about running technique, and for some pointers on how to improve.

The main things you should focus on when running are:

- Stand up tall

- Take short steps

- These two queues alone can make all the difference to your body.

Welcome to week three of your Calf Muscle Strain Rehab Plan

Great job getting through Week 2! Hopefully, you managed the running intervals without any pain or tightness in your calf. If you did feel any discomfort, don’t worry—it just means your body needs a bit more time. Take extra rest days if needed, and stick with the same number of reps until you can complete them comfortably. Remember, this plan might take longer than 10 weeks, and that’s totally okay. The most important thing is to listen to your body and progress at a pace your calf can handle.

This Week’s Running Intervals

We’ll continue to gradually build up your running time—as long as your calf is coping well.

Quick reminder of how the intervals work:

- Run 1 min / Walk 1 min x 7 reps Run for 1 minute at a relaxed, comfortable pace, then walk for 1 minute. Repeat the cycle 7 times in total.

Run 1 min / Walk 1 min x 7 reps Run for 1 minute at a relaxed, comfortable pace, then walk for 1 minute. Repeat the cycle 7 times in total.

If you notice any tightness or discomfort during a session:

- Stop immediately.

Stop immediately.

- Rest and do the stretching routine that day.

Rest and do the stretching routine that day.

- Try the same session again the following day.

Try the same session again the following day.

To move to the next level (e.g., 10 reps), you need to complete the current level twice with no pain or tightness. If symptoms return, stick with the current level a little longer until things feel good again.

This process is all about consistency and patience—it’s the best way to safely get back to full running!

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Did you watch last week’s running technique video?

The sooner you improve your running technique the better. It is a VITAL component in the quest to keeping your calf happy. If you missed it last week make sure you watch this video to learn how to run with good technique.

In the video, I mention the importance of cadence — that’s the number of steps you take per minute while running. If you want to dive deeper into what cadence is, how to measure it, and ways to improve it, check out THIS ARTICLE .

One of the most common mistakes runners make when trying to increase their cadence is running too fast just to match the beeps of their metronome. This leads to quick fatigue and makes it feel impossible to sustain the higher cadence for long. Watch the video below for a simple technique to control your pace without losing that quicker turnover.

Welcome to Week 4 of your Calf Muscle Strain Rehab Plan

You’re making great progress! This week, we’ll start increasing the frequency of your runs—an effective way to boost your total running volume while still keeping the intervals short and manageable. As always, it’s essential to monitor how your calf is responding and adjust accordingly. If you feel like you need extra rest days or prefer running on alternate days, that’s perfectly okay. It may extend the plan to 12–14 weeks instead of 10, but the priority is staying injury-free.

At the same time, continue working on your running technique. Keep focusing on posture and form—it takes time for these changes to feel natural, so be patient and consistent. Stick with the plan, listen to your body, and you’ll keep building strength and confidence with every step.

notes.text: Quick reminder from last week: A common mistake when increasing cadence is trying to run too fast just to keep up with the metronome. This usually leads to early fatigue and makes it hard to sustain. If you missed it, watch this video for some simple tips on how to keep your cadence high without picking up the pace too much.

Welcome to Week 5 of your Calf Muscle Strain Rehab Plan

Congratulations on making it to Week 5! By now, your calf should be feeling stronger, and your confidence is likely growing with each session. This week, we’ll continue to build on that progress by increasing the duration of your running intervals, while keeping the walking breaks at 1 minute to help manage fatigue and minimise tension. Don’t forget—your stretching and strength routines are just as vital as the running itself, so stay consistent with those. As always, listen to your body and allow extra recovery days when needed. Progress takes time, and you’re doing great—keep it going!

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 6 of your Calf Muscle Strain Rehab Plan

You’re officially past the halfway point—great work! Week 6 is all about building on the solid foundation you’ve laid so far. As we continue to increase your running interval volume, it’s more important than ever to stay focused on your technique. With longer intervals comes more fatigue, which can cause your form to slip—so remember the golden rule: stand tall and take short, quick steps .

If you haven’t checked your cadence recently, now’s the perfect time to revisit it and make sure you’re still on track. Keep up with your stretching and strength work too—these are the pieces of the puzzle that keep your body balanced and your calf on the road to full recovery. You’re doing brilliantly—stay patient, stay consistent, and keep moving forward!

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 7 of your Calf Muscle Strain Rehab Plan

Well done on making it to Week 7! You should be feeling stronger, and your calf muscle should be responding well to the progressive increase in running intervals. This week, we’ll continue to build on your running time, but as always, make sure to listen to your body and adjust if needed. Keep focusing on maintaining your running form, and stick with your strength and mobility exercises — they’ll continue to support your recovery. Great work so far!

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 8 of your Calf Muscle Strain Rehab Plan

You’ve come a long way—great job! By now, your calf should be feeling much stronger and more resilient. This week, we’re stepping things up with longer running intervals of up to 10 minutes, broken up with 1-minute walking breaks. You’re getting close to running continuously again, so stay focused and trust the process.

Next week, we’ll increase the total duration of your run/walk sessions to around 60 minutes, and by Week 10, you’ll be running non-stop. Just remember: your stretching and strength work is still a vital part of your recovery. Stick with it, stay patient, and keep doing what you’re doing—you’re nearly there!

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 9 of your Calf Muscle Strain Rehab Plan

Congratulations on making it to Week 9! Your consistency and commitment are really paying off—your calf is getting stronger, and your fitness is building back up. This week, you’ll be tackling a mix of 10, 12, and 15-minute running intervals, a great step toward running continuously.

Be sure to check your cadence a few times throughout the week and stay mindful of your form. Remember: stand tall and take short, quick steps. You’re doing an incredible job—just one more week to go!

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 10 of your Calf Muscle Strain Rehab Plan

Congratulations on reaching the final week! Getting here means you’ve stayed committed, followed the plan, and taken a huge step toward building a stronger, more resilient calf muscle. This week, we’ll be alternating between continuous runs and walk/run intervals. You’ve steadily increased your running volume over the past 10 weeks, but it’s important to remember—you’re not completely in the clear just yet.

Now more than ever, it’s vital to keep tuning in to how your body feels. Any new niggles or tightness should be taken seriously—don’t try to run through them. Respecting your body’s signals is the key to staying injury-free for the long haul.

To keep the progress going, I strongly recommend that you continue on to our 12-Week Base Training Plan . It is designed to gradually build your aerobic capacity while further developing your strength and stability. By the end of those 12 weeks, you’ll have a solid foundation to confidently return to racing, training harder, and chasing your next goal.

Read THIS ARTICLE to learn more about the benefits of base training

Well done again, and happy running!

Mark Green

glossary.definition: Watch THIS VIDEO to diagnose your calf muscle injury correctly. A calf muscle strain usually comes on 20 – 30 minutes into a run, it feels like a strong cramping sensation, and it feels like a line running down the middle or outside of your calf.

Watch THIS VIDEO to diagnose your calf muscle injury correctly. A calf muscle tear is usually caused by a sudden increase in force, like jumping. It feels like a ripping sensation across the inside of the calf muscle.

The plan has been carefully structured with built-in recovery days between each run. We begin with a “one day on, one day off” pattern, gradually progressing to two consecutive run days followed by a rest day. These recovery periods are essential for allowing your calf to adapt and reducing the risk of flare-ups. You’re welcome to adjust the specific days to fit your schedule—but be sure not to run more than two days in a row to give your body the rest it needs to keep progressing safely.
If you have a particularly busy or stressful week and haven’t been able to complete one of the runs, don’t try to play catch up. Continue where you left off when you have time.

All of the running in this program is done at an aerobic pace. Aerobic means “running with oxygen”, which means running at a pace where you can comfortably carry out a conversation in full sentences. Don’t run so slowly that it feels unnatural and therefore effects your technique, but don’t run too quickly either. Run at a comfortable natural pace that allows you to breathe easily.

The 15-minute stretching routine is a key part of your success with this program. It’s designed to release tension in your lower back and hips while improving mobility in your sciatic nerve—an often overlooked factor behind recurring calf strains. If you skip this daily stretching routine, you’re much more likely to keep battling the same injury.

Starting in Week 2, we’ll be adding a 10-minute strength and stability workout to your routine. These sessions are designed to build core strength and improve hip and pelvic stability—two essential elements for staying injury-free over the long term. Don’t skip them—they’re just as important as the running in this plan.
